articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the issuance of an amended Iran-related General License on October 29, 2026.
This amendment is part of OFAC's ongoing review and adjustment of its sanctions programs to ensure they remain current and effective.
Further details regarding the scope and specific changes within this amended general license are expected to be closely scrutinized by entities involved in Iran-related transactions.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: On October 28, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities in North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
These actions aim to counter illicit activities and human rights abuses in these regions, reinforcing U.S. foreign policy objectives.
The specific individuals and entities designated, and the reasons for their inclusion, will be detailed in the official OFAC publication.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Settles with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, has reached a settlement agreement with OFAC for $1,529,685 regarding apparent violations of Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer.

MMZA was deemed a blocked person by operation of law due to its majority ownership by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey, a designated Russian state-owned defense company, even though MMZA itself was not on the SDN List at the time of the transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced amendments to several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026.
These revisions, affecting FAQs 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53, aim to update guidance on blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC.

The amendments clarify distinctions between blocking and rejecting transactions, address reporting requirements for blocked property and rejected transactions through the OFAC Reporting System (ORS), and differentiate between customer inquiries and actual payment instructions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran and Russia-Related General Licenses, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: On October 21, 2026, OFAC announced new Iran-related designations and the issuance of Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses.
Concurrently, OFAC also announced the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.
These actions reflect a dynamic adjustment of U.S. sanctions policy, with further details on the specific designations, removals, and general licenses available on the OFAC website.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026.
These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses, providing guidance on authorized transactions.
This action underscores the U.S. government's commitment to protecting American intellectual property globally through sanctions measures.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: On October 16, 2026, OFAC issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and an updated Frequently Asked Question.
This amendment aims to refine existing sanctions policy concerning Venezuela, potentially impacting certain sectors or transactions.
The updated guidance will be crucial for entities engaging in activities related to Venezuela to ensure ongoing compliance.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities in Iran and Cuba, Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities in Iran and Cuba on October 15, 2026.
Alongside these designations, OFAC issued new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions to provide guidance on authorized activities.
These actions reflect continued U.S. efforts to exert pressure on these regimes while providing specific avenues for permissible transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: On October 14, 2026, the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation.
This action indicates a potential shift in U.S. policy towards certain individuals or entities previously sanctioned in connection with Venezuela.
The specific details of the removed designation will be important for stakeholders monitoring changes in the Venezuela sanctions program.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting individuals and entities involved in counter narcotics and counter terrorism activities on October 13, 2026.
These designations are part of ongoing U.S. efforts to disrupt global illicit networks and protect national security.
The specific targets of these designations will be detailed in official OFAC releases, highlighting the U.S. commitment to combating these threats.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Fined $1,529,685 by OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to settle its potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a Russian missile and air defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), which was majority-owned by a designated Russian state-owned company.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious, noting the company's reckless disregard for U.S. sanctions requirements and failure to conduct sufficient diligence.

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930 in Sanctions Violations
body: Bank of America, N.A. has agreed to an $11,662,930 settlement with OFAC for 475 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs, including those targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.

The apparent violations stemmed from issues such as processing payments involving blocked banks, failing to prioritize alerts for sanctioned customers, and mishandling business accounts associated with blocked persons.
OFAC determined that the apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement amount reflects no reduction for remedial measures or cooperation.

articles.headline: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics Fined $175,015 by OFAC for Counter Narcotics Sanctions Violations
body: Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, a California-based freight forwarder, has agreed to pay $175,015 to settle apparent violations of OFAC counter narcotics sanctions and reporting obligations.

The violations involved arranging the shipment of equipment from a designated Chinese supplier, Youli Technology Development Co., Ltd., which had changed its name but retained other SDN-listed identifiers.

OFAC determined the violations were non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, citing Pegasus's reckless disregard for sanctions requirements and initial failure to fully respond to an administrative subpoena.

articles.headline: Individual Settles with OFAC for $1,427,230 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: An individual has agreed to pay $1,427,230 to settle potential civil liability for 39 apparent violations of the Iranian Transactions and Sanctions Regulations.

The violations, which occurred between June 2019 and July 2021, involved providing management consulting and advisory services to Iranian companies, receiving Iranian-origin dividends into U.S. bank accounts, and purchasing property in Iran.
OFAC classified the apparent violations as egregious and noted that they had not been voluntarily self-disclosed, emphasizing its ongoing enforcement campaign against Iran sanctions violators.

articles.headline: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc. Fined $60,764 for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Rice Lake Weighing Systems, Inc., a Wisconsin-based manufacturer, has agreed to pay $60,764 to settle eight apparent violations of OFAC sanctions on Iran.

The violations occurred when its Italian subsidiary, Dini Argeo S.r.l., exported weighing equipment to Iran through a distributor in the United Arab Emirates, despite being aware of the ultimate destination.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and non-egregious, highlighting the importance of clear communication and oversight for foreign subsidiaries regarding sanctions compliance.

articles.headline: FTI Consulting, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,050,000 Over Russia Sanctions
body: FTI Consulting, Inc., a Washington D.C.-based international advisory firm, has agreed to pay $1,050,000 to settle apparent violations of OFAC sanctions targeting Russia's financial sector.
Between April 2019 and May 2021, FTI indirectly dealt in prohibited debt of VTB Bank OAO, a Russian state-owned bank on OFAC's Sectoral Sanctions Identification List.
OFAC determined that FTI's conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, emphasizing that it is prohibited to do indirectly what one cannot do directly.

articles.headline: Adani Enterprises Limited Fined $275,000,000 by OFAC for Iran Sanctions Violations
body: Adani Enterprises Limited (AEL), an India-based multinational, has agreed to pay $275,000,000 to settle 32 apparent violations of OFAC's Iran sanctions regulations.
From November 2023 to June 2025, AEL caused U.S. financial institutions to process payments for Iranian-origin liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) disguised as Omani and Iraqi product.
OFAC deemed the violations egregious and not voluntarily self-disclosed, citing AEL's commercial sophistication and the harm to U.S. foreign policy objectives.

articles.headline: TradeStation Securities, Inc. Settles with OFAC for $1,110,661 Over Sanctions Violations
body: TradeStation Securities, Inc., a Florida-headquartered brokerage firm, has agreed to pay $1,110,661 to settle 481 apparent violations of multiple sanctions programs.
For nearly a year, from June 2021 to June 2022, TradeStation provided investment services to customers located in Iran, Syria, and the Crimea region of Ukraine due to compliance control failures.
OFAC determined the apparent violations were non-egregious and voluntarily self-disclosed, and the settlement reflects significant remedial measures implemented by TradeStation.

articles.headline: Individual Fined $3,777,000 by OFAC for Syrian Sanctions Violations
body: A U.S. citizen residing abroad has agreed to pay $3,777,000 to settle potential civil liability for 20 apparent violations of the Syrian Sanctions Regulations.
The violations occurred between 2018 and 2021, involving activities prohibited under the Syrian sanctions program.
This enforcement action underscores OFAC's continued focus on individuals who violate U.S. sanctions, even when residing outside the United States.

articles.headline: IMG Academy, LLC Settles with OFAC for $1,720,000 Over Counter Narcotics Sanctions
body: IMG Academy, LLC, a Florida-based academic and athletic training facility, has agreed to pay $1,720,000 to settle 89 apparent violations of OFAC counternarcotics sanctions.

Between 2019 and 2025, IMG Academy entered into tuition enrollment agreements and processed payments with two individuals designated under the Foreign Narcotics Kingpin Designation Act due to their ties to a sanctioned Mexican drug cartel.
OFAC determined that the conduct was non-egregious and not voluntarily disclosed, emphasizing the importance for academic institutions to implement robust sanctions screening and compliance programs.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
